notes: HOW THIS WAS BUILT: standard-language entries come from Wiktionary tags (via kaikki.org), Tanzanian street slang from Reuster-Jahn and Kiessling 2006, hate-speech terms from the Kenyan NCIC 2022 list, and real-use checks from the JamiiForums dataset. Counts and sources are in the sources array. The scam array is NOT from any corpus: it is typical comment-spam wording written from general knowledge, so treat it as a starting list. DATASET NOTE: the JamiiForums labels are unreliable (label 0 holds many abusive posts such as punguwani, wanatombwa, vilaza), so usage was judged from the text, not from the label. ABUSIVE IN ONE CONTEXT, ORDINARY IN ANOTHER (included, expect some harmless holds): shoga/mashoga/ushoga (shoga is also a normal word for a woman's close female friend, and ushoga can mean close friendship between women, but in Tanzanian comments it is mostly a homophobic slur; kept so it is held); basha (king in cards); mavi (animal dung); kunya (to defecate, vulgar); jinga/mjinga/ujinga/upuuzi/upumbavu (mild, also used in serious argument); mhuni/wahuni (news word for thugs); mkora (rascal); jahili (also 'ignorant', jahiliyya); mkundu (anus, medical); punyeto (standard word for masturbation); nyege (lust, vulgar); kafiri/makafiri (religious word, neutral inside some Muslim writing, but a slur and on the NCIC list); mzinzi/mwasherati/uasherati (religious wording); zeruzeru (very common media word for a person with albinism, regarded as derogatory by many advocates); kilema/kiwete/kibete (dictionary words that are often used as insults); lofa; kicheche (also polecat; womaniser); poko; mamako and babako (your mother/father, usually a curse opener but can be neutral) and the phrases mama yako and baba yako (user asked for them; they will also hold harmless comments such as 'salamu kwa mama yako'); madoadoa (also just 'spots'); waende kwao; potelea mbali; huna maana; kaa jikoni; nitakupiga (also 'nitakupiga picha' or 'nitakupiga simu' = I will photograph/phone you); nitakumaliza (sports banter); mbwa koko (stray dog). LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE (ordinary words, or ordinary-looking words that are also slurs): mbuzi, punda, mbwa, nguruwe, kondoo, kima ('kima cha chini' = minimum amount), mnyama, nyani, ng'ombe, mende, kupe (tick) and kwekwe (weeds, both on the NCIC list) appear ONLY inside insult phrases like 'mbwa wewe'; nyau (also 'cat'); chizi (also 'cheese', and mchizi = friend); boga (pumpkin); ziro (zero); ubwabwa/bwabwa (rice; homosexual in street slang); choko, mshumaa, chakula, kaka poa (street-slang euphemisms for a gay man, but everyday words); shamba (bare stem of mshamba, so only mshamba/washamba/ushamba/kishamba are listed); mchongo/chongo (mchongo = a plan; chongo = one-eyed, dropped because the prefix stripper would turn mchongo into chongo); mluzi/luzi (whistle; only kiluzi kept); shangingi (luxury SUV, also 'prostitute' in slang); kiberenge (train, also 'prostitute'); kirukanjia (nightjar); maharage ya mbeya, mama huruma, dege la jeshi (real beans, a common name, a military plane); msamba (perineum); hayawani (animal; only inside 'wewe hayawani'); kibirikizi (announcer); mbilikimo (pygmy, ethnographic); maamuma; fuska; kichaa (rabies is 'kichaa cha mbwa'; only inside phrases and as vichaa); kazi ya nyumbani (HOMEWORK, very common on an education blog, so only longer job-spam phrases are in scam); ngono (sex; neutral in news and health text), lawiti/kulawiti and 'kinyume cha maumbile' (legal and news terms), kinembe, kisimi, uume, uke, matiti, matako, makalio, korodani, kende, shahawa, manii, kukojoa (anatomical or medical); mbakaji, jambazi, mwizi, mwongo, mnafiki, mjeuri, mkorofi, mhalifu, fisadi, mpagani, walokole, magaidi, hawara, mchepuko (common but not abuse on their own); jamba (fart, but also door-post); mshindo (bang; the dataset's 'nyege mshindo'); chupi, gashi, kimeo, mbovu (slang for women but also underwear, pretty, broken, rotten); kujiuza (can mean self-promotion in career texts, so only anajiuza/wanajiuza/unajiuza/mnajiuza). NOT SAFE AS STEMS: malaya (Himalaya contains it), msenge/wasenge/kisenge (msengenyaji, wasengenya = gossip), mkundu (medical text), nitakupiga (see above). The stems array only holds strings I checked against 17,739 Wiktionary Swahili headwords plus all forms and the dataset vocabulary; they occur only inside their own inflections. Entries that are in stems are not repeated in words. PREFIX-STRIP CHECK: I ran the matcher's one-level prefix stripping (m, mw, wa, ki, vi, u, n, ny) over the same vocabulary; the only ordinary words that would be caught were rare derived forms of listed words. UNVERIFIED OR LOW-CONFIDENCE ENTRIES (meaning inferred or seen in one source only): kumamayo; kubabako and kubabae (usage confirmed 39 and 30 times in real posts, meaning inferred from the pattern kuma + ya + baba yako/yake); kumamae (pattern of kumamake); the l-spellings filwa, kufilwa, kafilwe, ufilwe, ukifilwa (Tanzanians swap r and l; unafilwa and ukifilwa were seen in real posts, the rest are the same verb); qumamake, qumamaque, qumamae, qumamako (k to q dodge, qumamaque seen once); hanisi (s-spelling of hanithi, seen twice); msenzi (assumed sh to s dodge); malaia; mpumbafu, pumbafu family (v to f; mpumbafu seen once); katombwer (typo seen 7 times); bozi, bozibozi, juha (Wiktionary only, rare); zoba, mbwiga, mnyela, poyoyo, mgoroko, mento, boka, shwaini, mbushi, kiluzi, mlupo, kolboksi, shankupe, kitombi (Reuster-Jahn and Kiessling 2006 only, 2000-2006 Dar es Salaam slang, may be dated); vilaza/kilaza (meaning 'dunce' read from real forum use, not in a dictionary I opened); vichaa; tahira (variant of taahira, seen in real use); baradhuli (Wiktionary: simpleton, riffraff); poko (Wiktionary, Sheng only); mnanuka/unanuka (regular forms of 'to stink'); dinya/kudinya (Wiktionary Sheng, rare); dada poa (Wiktionary says prostitute, but the same words are also a friendly address); jamvi la wageni (Wiktionary only); kunyea; kujamba; the regular verb forms nitakuchapa, nitakupasua, nitakukomesha, nitawaua and the like (grammatical, not individually seen); nitakukongoli (the paper writes kong'oli; apostrophe removed); the self-harm forms jiue, jinyonge, kajiue, ukajiue, kajinyonge, ukajinyonge (jiue and ukafe seen in real use, jinyonge is the regular reflexive of nyonga 'to hang'); mungu akuadhibu and mungu akulaani; wakristo ni nguruwe and waislamu ni mbuzi (I could not confirm any source that documents a nguruwe/mbuzi religious insult pairing; nguruwe as 'despicable person' is in Wiktionary; kept as patterns, drop them if unwanted); dini ya magaidi; mbwa koko; ngamia wewe (Wiktionary: ngamia = idiot, derogatory); sura yako mbaya. COVERAGE GAPS: Sheng and Kenyan street insults are thin because no open Sheng insult list was found (the 2003 Sheng-English Dictionary itself was not opened; kumbafu, ngamwe, ngati, mburula, mchome could not be verified and were left out). Other Kenyan languages (Kikuyu, Luo, Kalenjin, Kamba) are only covered by the NCIC terms kihii and mwiji. Insults based on tribe names in Tanzania were not found in any source I could open. No list of Tanzanian religious slurs beyond kafiri was found. Anything below 6 letters can only go in words, so short dodges such as 'mbo' were not added. SPELLING RULES USED: lowercase, apostrophes removed (ng'ombe is ngombe, kong'oli is kongoli), hyphens turned into spaces (mwana haramu appears as a phrase; mwanaharamu is a stem), no digits or symbols, repeated letters not listed (the matcher handles them).
